{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"If you buy a device, you expect to own it. You expect your device to answer to you, to keep its functions when you carry it home, and to remain useful after the receipt has gone into the recycling. You’re buying a glowing rectangle, not renting one from a distant landlord. You’re buying an object (with a screen, a battery, and a tiny computer inside it) whose capabilities were part of the bargain. That seems obvious, until the maker reaches through the network and switches one off.

When we talk about ownership, we mean control, and our laws and customs have usually treated control as something that travels with a sale. You’ve paid the price – you’ve accepted the object – you can decide how to use it. A maker who can revoke a feature after the transaction has kept a veto over your purchase. What kind of ownership leaves the seller holding the switch?

The trick is easy to miss because the object still sits on your desk. You can touch it, charge it, and admire the polished casing. Yet a disabled feature turns the device into a stage set: convincing from the audience, hollow backstage. The network connection becomes a leash, and the terms of service become the hand holding it. I think that’s the point at which a consumer product stops behaving like a thing you own and starts behaving like access permitted on loan.

Of course, remote controls can serve legitimate safety purposes. A security update may close a real vulnerability, and a manufacturer may need a narrow way to respond to an emergency. But a safety valve isn’t a blank check – it’s a distinction between repairing a product and redesigning the bargain after the buyer has left the store. If the feature can vanish because a server says so, the buyer has acquired a dependency, not full control.

Imagine buying a refrigerator whose cold setting works only while the brand approves the grocery list. The compressor, door, and shelves remain physical property, but the temperature belongs to an account in somebody else’s cloud. The owner could keep the machine spotless and pay every bill on time; a remote decision would still change what the object can do. That’s a refrigerator only in name. It’s a subscription wearing a metal costume.

I’ve seen this argument reduced to a technicality, as though the only question were whether the casing remains in the buyer’s kitchen. I don’t buy that. We’re talking about power: who can alter the object, who can withdraw its functions, and who must ask permission to recover them (in plain English). When we accept a sale that leaves the maker with a kill switch, we turn a durable exchange into a temporary grant. The product is presented as owned, while the meaningful parts remain somewhere else. That’s the bullshit hidden inside the word “ownership.”

Here is the policy line I would draw: a maker may fix a defect, but removal of a paid-for capability should require a fresh agreement. The distinction should appear in law, contracts, and design. If a feature is advertised, sold, and central to the device’s ordinary use, the owner should receive a durable way to keep it working (even if the network disappears). A company can offer new services, but it can’t convert yesterday’s purchase into tomorrow’s ransom. That is a sale – control, responsibility, and continuity.

This matters beyond gadgets. The loss of a feature means losing the ability to plan around the thing purchased. Customers face a price increase, a policy change, or a corporate decision that arrives without a new sale (and the customer absorbs the risk). The bargain has been inverted: the customer carries the cost, and the maker retains the exit. A device can sit in a home for years while its essential abilities remain contingent on a remote permission.

The demand is simple: ownership should survive a remote command. Repair rights, local functionality, and clear limits on post-sale control belong in the rules governing connected products. New software can improve a device, but its original capabilities should remain available to the person who paid for them, subject to genuine safety constraints. Every maker may keep improving its products; every buyer should keep the substance of the bargain. A device that can be switched off after sale is still useful, perhaps even excellent, but it is access with a receipt attached.","omitted":[{"habit":"opponents-allies-sources / o12: named attribution, embedded quotation, linked authority, or precise opponent/source summary","why":"The request supplies no verified source, named opponent position, or quotation to attribute."}],"refused":""}
